author: Italo Calvino
introFa: کتاب «Invisible Cities» نوشته Italo Calvino یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Invisible Cities»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: TORKE: Rapture (Percussion Concerto); An American Abroad; Jasper. Colin Currie (perc), Royal Scottish National Orchestra c. Marin Alsop. Naxos American Classics 8.5599167 Michael Torke’s music is distinguished by a considerable energy and great feeling for orchestral colour, both of which are in ample evidence on this disc. In these three works, written between 1998 and 2001, he shows himself to be broadening stylistically and evidencing a vitality that may fairly be described as life-enhancing. On the face of it, it is the percussion concerto Rapture that most represents the established style that is regarded as quintessential Torke; here are the spiky melodies, motoric ostinati and blocks of orchestral colour that have been observable since his early output. But in writing for the percussion medium Torke takes the opportunity to explore a Yeatsian vein of inspiration; he takes his rise from the late poem News for a Delphic Oracle, where an orgiastic dance brings about an effect that is simultaneously violent and ritual- istic, inviting the listener to submit to the over- powering rhythm. Torke shows this in a piece where each of the three movements concen- trates on a different percussive section – drums and woods in the first, then mallets and metals in turn, with jazzy and increasingly complex rhythms that offset the soloist against the orchestra whilst avoiding the conventional display of the concerto form. In An American Abroad, Torke’s style assumes a somewhat softer edge, and there are times indeed when the music seems on the verge of breaking into the big theme from Rhapsody in Blue. This kaleidoscopic piece is a depiction of the varied impressions of a journey from Torke’s homeland, with much lively and attractive writing that is highly accessible without being simplistic. Although there are certainly moments when Gershwin is a dominant influence, the harmonic world is all Torke’s, concentrating as ever on the warping of tonality to a greater or lesser extent, but here tending towards the warmth of jazz-influenced chords that are ameliorated by irregular and often surprising phrase-lengths. This is a well-crafted piece that gives popularity a good name. Jasper was written overlooking Lake Superior, and is superbly written for large orchestra, often treated with great delicacy. It seems cut from the same cloth as An American Abroad, an optimistic, exuberant paean to the great outdoors. The seven-note theme makes use of each note of the diatonic scale once only, then recurs in various guises; ‘changes, genuflections and other prod- ding’ as Torke puts it in his liner notes. The result is what might with some fairness be called a tone-poem, and is a work that deserves to be heard often in the concert hall (it might even, with good fortune, become a Proms favourite). A splendidly played and recorded disc, this is an important release for Torke and shows him as a composer at the height of his powers. John Kersey STOCKHAUSEN: Michael’s Farewell; plus works by ANDREW POWELL, TIM SOUSTER and ROGER SMALLEY. John Wallace (tpt), Andew Powell, (live electronics). Deux-Elles DXL 1039 JONATHAN HARVEY: Oeuvres pour violoncelle: Curve with Plateaux; Ricercare una melodia; Three Sketches; Chant; Advaya. Benjamin Carat, (vlc). Assai 222242- MU750 The trumpeting of John Wallace, along with tape/delay or other live electronics, is what is chiefly showcased on the Deux-Elles CD. From the big lettering on the cover, though, you’d be forgiven for thinking this was a disk mainly of Stockhausen (perhaps, shrinking violet that he is, it was felt he needed a bit of boosting...); his contribution actually turns out to be but a modest curio. But the three other composers represented were all at some point his students or assistants, and in any case the whole can be heard as an interesting comment on the relationship of electronics to musical culture and musical tech- niques over recent decades. Andrew Powell’s Plasmogeny II (1999), and The Transistor Radio of St Narcissus (1982/3) by the late Tim Souster seem conceptually kindred, perhaps not too surprisingly, given the composers’ common involvement in the group Intermodulation, which prèmiered the earlier work. Both pieces make the same stylistic   69 Tempo 57 (224) 69–82 © 2003 Cambridge University Press DOI: 10.1017/S0040298203000172 Printed in the United Kingdom https://www.cambridge.org/core/terms. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0040298203290173

journey, from stasis and fragment to movement and euphony; even more specifically, from esoteric to exoteric. Over the course of about ten minutes, the Powell proceeds from its initial spectral – indeed sometimes sphincteral – trumpet sounds, set against a dirty white-noise background which rapidly becomes a chordal synth pad. The music moves purposefully, even menacingly, towards its conclusion, in which an almost Stanley Clarke- esque fretless bass line romps the piece home, underneath roto-tomming Koto sounds and Dizzy-ing trumpet virtuosity, to the final shame- less glitz of its B flat major ending. The Souster embarks on a very similar trip from studio to street. It, too, starts in the primeval soup of sparse-textured electronics, from which eventually emerges a walking bass line pulsing along under increasingly jazzy riffs (like the Powell, it ends up tweaking an udder of the B flat cow, to misquote Brahms). That Narcissus does not match the flourish and flow of Plasmogeny II is not a question of the Souster’s being simply a less poppy, more serious exploration of electronics (on the contrary, some of its principal sounds appear as presets on the old Yamaha TG33). And it’s really not a bad work, being at times redolent in its sensitivity to atmosphere of some of those wonderful early Ussachevsky & Leuning essays in the genre. But name three electronic works that don’t go on just a bit too long? It’s this apparently irresistible compulsion to make pieces evolu- tionary, gradual transformations in which shifting textures are the vernacular. That – and 20 years of the medium loosening up – is the difference here: the Souster takes an age to get going (at nearly 25 minutes it’s 21/2 times the length of the Powell), and it lacks the ultimately exponential excite- ment-curve of the later work. The remaining two pieces also form a compar- able pair: both are solely for multiple trumpet sounds; both are austerely contrapuntal. Roger Smalley’s Echo III (1978) pits a live trumpet against two differently-staggered delayed recordings of itself, at some point achieving a sort of, well, inevitable aggregation – rather than a musical climax, exactly. And to conclude the CD, as adver- tised – STOCKHAUSEN. Michaels-Abschied, written for 5 trumpets (here Wallace overdub- bing), is envoi to his opera Donnerstag: some may remember it serenading exeunt-ing operagoers stereophonically from the rooftops of WC2 at the Covent Garden production some years ago. It is pure systems music: each player has a different, short, pattern, and each keeps repeating that pattern. Then stops. End of story. But though the theory is strict Reich, the result is strict 1980s-undergraduate-style (=nice-ish idea,  70 MUSIC OF TODAY Thursday 10 April 6pm Royal Festival Hall ANTHONY GILBERT Beastly Jingles Réflections, Rose Nord Vasanta with Dancing Martyn Brabbins conductor Marie Vassiliou soprano Presented by Julian Anderson in conversation with Anthony Gilbert Tuesday 29 April 6pm Royal Festival Hall MICHAEL JARRELL Prisme Music for a while Martyn Brabbins conductor Maya Iwabuchi violin Presented by Julian Anderson in conversation with Michael Jarrell Thursday 19 June 6pm Royal Festival Hall New compositions by post-graduate students from the Royal College of Music, inspired by works of art in the National Gallery Garry Walker conductor Presented by Julian Anderson in conversation with the young composers Entrance is free - no ticket required! supported by the RPS https://www.cambridge.org/core/terms. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0040298203290173

featurelessly overstretched). Do you remember that Laurel & Hardy film where they sit in their char-a-banc outside the house, endlessly chorusing goodbyes, without ever being in danger of actually getting anywhere? Michael’s Farewell is a bit like that, only not as funny... By coincidence, Ricercare una melodia, from Jonathan Harvey’s recent CD of cello works, began life scored just like the Smalley, for trumpet and tape delay. And there all resem- blance between these two CDs begins. Like the Wallace collection, this, also, is a group of pieces for solo instrument with or without electronic intervention/involvement: it, too, raises issues about the nature, and influence, of composition with electronics. Indeed, possibly the most inter- esting number here, conceptually at least, Advaya, of 1994, explores and blurs the bound- aries between instrumental and electronic domains. But even in the music for solo acoustic cello, much of Harvey’s sound-world and its tech- niques seem close to the spirit of studio- engineered tones; the Scelsian preoccupation with timbral changes on single notes (in Curve with Plateaux, for instance) appearing to seek justification from the transformational process itself, from mutation of aural phenomena alone, without recourse to other aspects or principles of composition. (This within a genre in which J.S.Bach’s examples prove comprehensively that monody need not mean monotony...) Among the intentions of this music, we read, are ‘to bypass central voices of the classical- romantic repertoire’ and to employ ‘mercurial gestures implying something dashed off with the immediacy of a sketch’. Success on both counts, but not without cost, perhaps. The capricious bursts of scordatura’d gratings, body-tappings, and extremes of register in these pieces all fit Harvey’s description of the cello becoming gourmet of acoustic curiosities. But they run the risk of rolling across the listener’s palate simply as a concatenation of amuse-gueules, suggesting either indulgence, or a want of that deceptively rare art in shaping through which a group of sound-events becomes discernibly a piece. These are issues familiar to modern music in general – but, surely, to electronic composition in particular, where the canvas starts freer of history’s trace, and the trap of confounding novelty and experiment with finished article yawns wide. All the more encouraging, perhaps, that Andrew Powell’s Plasmogeny II, the most recent – and the least dated-sounding – of all the music from these CDs, seems to have learnt lessons from the history of electronics – to say nothing of it representing a musical and telling metaphor for the migration of electronics from province of the boffin to plaything of the re- mixer. Mark Cromar LACHENMANN: Schwankungen am Rand; Mouvement (- vor der Erstarrung); “...zwei Gefühle...”, Musik mit Leonardo. Ensemble Modern, Ensemble Modern Orchestra, c. Peter Eötvös. ECM New Series 1789, 461949-2. Mouvement (-vor der Erstarrung); “...zwei Gefühle...”, Musik mit Leonardo; Consolation I; Consolation II. Klangforum Wien c. Hans Zender; Schola Heidelberg, ensemble aisthesis, c. Walter Nussbaum. Kairos 0012202KAI. We tend to think that what is unfamiliar today will be common place tomorrow in one big wave of historical assimilation. By now, the music of one of the major figures of post-war German music, Helmut Lachenmann (b. 1935), should have had sufficient time for this assumption to take effect. Yet it has lost none of its surprise element. Shocking it is probably no longer, and the territory of estranged instrumental treat- ment is, if not commonplace, certainly some- thing like familiar ground. His works, however, remain one big playful mystery. Those grateful listeners stimulated by the composer’s guided game of acoustic adventure, destabilization and discovery (how much safer can you get than in a concert hall?), within a framework abstract enough to allow for innumerable references, love his music. Those who prefer to operate with more familiar and defined objets react strongly against it. Vive la difference! Over the last couple of years almost two dozen new CDs with Lachenmann’s works have been issued, no less than five of them from the laudable Austrian label Kairos (www.kairos-music.com). Their last Lachenmann CD, with his opera (the composer calls it ‘music in pictures’) The Little Match Girl has just been honoured with one of the coveted German Record Review Awards for 2002.1 Kairos’s Lachenmann CD with Klangforum Wien performing his two ensemble pieces Mouvement (- vor der Erstarrung) [Mouvement (- before paral- ysis)] and “…zwei Gefühle…”, Musik mit Leonardo [“…two feelings…”, Music with Leonardo] was released in 2001. What must be one of 1 Das Mädchen mit dem Schwefelhölzern (Kairos 0012282KAI) was reviewed by Arnold Whittall in Tempo 222 (October 2002), pp.35–6 (Ed.)  71 https://www.cambridge.org/core/terms. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0040298203290173

Lachenmann’s finest works to date, Mouvement, was thus at last available again after the 1985 LP recording on Harmonia Mundi sold out quite some time ago. Last year, ECM released a CD with the same two ensemble works played by no less prestigious a group of players than the Ensemble Modern. Although the ECM disc reached the market only recently, the Ensemble Modern recordings date back to 1994, before Klangforum recorded for Kairos. It was the Ensemble Modern under Peter Eötvös who premièred Mouvement in the mid- 1980s, recorded it for Harmonia Mundi and have toured it extensively ever since. Mouvement is the kind of work which allows the Ensemble’s very special expertise and inclinations to blossom, and one could be forgiven for thinking that this has been one of those rare near-perfect symbioses between players’ interpretation and composer’s intentions. What a delight to see the Ensemble Modern take to the studios again to archive their accumulated experiences a decade after their first recording! They negotiate the rhythmic and metric difficulties with breathtaking and self- confident ease; their command of the various unusual playing techniques is outstanding; and their sheer virtuosity in bringing all the elements of this soundscape together deserves absolute and unqualified praise: there is a scratching and shuffling, a whispering and hissing, a brushing, scuffling, rattling, flicking, screeching, popping, whipping, trembling, tapping, oscillating, pulsing, fidgeting, wobbling, bubbling, exploding, gallop- ing, boiling, chasing, stumbling, scrabbling – and there is silence as the defining space for these well-choreographed and manipulated musical gestures directed by the composer with a fine and complex sense for the active forces in music such as energy, contrast, variety, repetition, surprise and the like. Klangforum Wien has also been an advocate of Lachenmann’s Mouvement in the concert hall. The comparison of their recording with the Ensemble Modern’s interpretation is nothing if not favourable. Accuracy, virtuosity and the joy of playing communicate through Klangforum’s interpretation with equal force. If anything, the recording quality of the Kairos CD appears a little more flexible, seemingly ‘zooming in’ with the microphone to individual players when the texture is very dry, thus reproducing a little more of the mysterious resonances which die away after a gesture. At other times, the Kairos producers preferred a ‘distant’ approach when the rattling infects the whole ensemble. The Klangforum recording of Mouvement is ca. 20 seconds shorter than Ensemble Modern’s. Someone has obviously ‘tidied up’ one or two passages between the two recording sessions. There is no doubt that Lachenmann’s compo- sitional approach has changed between Mouvement and his second ensemble piece “…zwei Gefühle…” from 1992, again first performed by the Ensemble Modern. The surface of “…zwei Gefühle” is just as ruffled with overtones as ever – maybe a little more resonant – but one gets the impression that the spatial metaphors from modern visual art, increasingly applied to music void of traditional tension- release developments, have given Lachenmann some kind of new framework to design his musical soundscapes more intuitively and spaciously, rather than relying so much on his logarithmically conceived time-lines which can been seen determining the length of passages in many of his older manuscript pages. In “…zwei Gefühle...” there is the added dimension of the spoken text extract from Leonardo da Vinci’s ‘desire of knowledge’. It is delivered by two speakers supposedly representing two sides of the mind. The text is almost continuously present and is to be recited in a stumbling and searching syllabification on the same mono- chrome tone. Ueli Wiget and Frank Ollu on the ECM CD display an almost angry delight in the added consonants, compared to Lachenmann who himself recorded both speaker parts for Kairos with a gentler tone. The subject of searching for knowledge is also apparent in Lachenmann’s early piece for voices Consolation I and II (1968/69), from a time when he began to develop the musical language that he was to describe as ‘musique conrète instrumentale’. Compared to the later pieces, Consolation I sounds positively lush. Lachenmann’s growing sensitivity to and preoccupation with the life of resonances is only taking effect in the second choral work. Yet already in Consolation I, Lachenmann’s choice of text (Ernst Toller’s ‘… recognize yourself’ is one of the understandable key words) and musical disposition betray the composer’s restlessness and his determined attempt to wring out a new dimension from the presumed world of musical articulation and form. Fine performances indeed by Schola Heidelberg (and the players of aesthesis) under Walter Nussbaum. The first and longest piece on the ECM disc, Schwankungen am Rand, [Fluctuations on the Edge] has not ranked among the top ten most performed Lachenmann works so far, yet this recording by the Ensemble Modern Orchestra under Eötvos might change all that. It is pure, unadulterated Lachenmann from the mid-1970s,  72 https://www.cambridge.org/core/terms. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0040298203290173

in full command of an ingenious orchestral body (despite the subtitle ‘for brass and strings’ the line-up also includes 4 metal sheets whose thun- ders certainly colour the piece, 2 electronic guitars, 2 pianos – but no horn and tubas or celli and basses). Delicious anger and extraordinary musical skill characterize this tapestry of gestures, striving so hard to make the resonances last. The musicians are obviously very much at home in this sound-world and can concentrate on the job at hand: to play music seriously. At this point it is important to state the simple truth that Lachenmann’s music on CD could only ever be part of the whole story. True as it may be for any composition written originally for the concert hall, in the case of Lachenmann, the lack of visual cueing and the technical limita- tions to reproducing the acutely subtle move- ments and interferences of sound waves in space invariably leave his music stripped of an essential dimension on CD. The producers of both CDs have obviously tried their utmost to recreate some of the magic, and you simply could not ask for better recordings of Lachenmann’s works, but the result should not be misunderstood as a substitute for the real McLachenmann. Elke Hockings BERMEL: Soul Garden; Wanderings; Coming Together; Turning; Theme and Absurdities; Mulatash Stomp; SchiZm; Quartet. Borromeo String Quartet, Derek Bermel (cl.), Christopher Taylor (pno), Heleen Hulst (vn), Fred Sherry (vc), Theo Primis (hn), Frank Morelli (bsn), Bob Ingliss (ob), Tara Helen O’Connor (fl). CRI- Emergency Music CD 895. Newcomers to Derek Bermel’s music will find him among the most eclectic of the younger generation of American composers, with a stylistic pedigree that embraces both Western and non-Western influences. A virtuoso clarinet- tist with deep roots in both the jazz and classical spheres, Bermel also owes much to gospel tradi- tions and has studied the lobi xylophone (gyil) in Ghana, the uillean pipes in Dublin and Thracian folk style in Bulgaria. This disc showcases Bermel’s chamber output, with the composer performing as clarinettist on a number of the tracks listed. A theme running through a number of the works is that of the representation of speech or vocalization, a persistent concern of Bermel, in such a way that, whilst preserving the abstraction of his epigram- matic titles, he is nevertheless able to suggest the programmatic associations of dialogue or gesture, often through the use of portamenti coupled with sinuous jazz rhythms. This is notable in Coming Together for clarinet and cello, consisting entirely of glissandi, in which the lowing of the cello at the opening is answered by the almost feline clarinet, setting up an argu- ment that gradually sees the two instrumental lines coalesce into a single parallel movement. A piece which is at times (surely intentionally) laugh-out-loud humorous, it is difficult to conceive this as anything other than a tour de force of performance art, where the gestural vocabulary is writ large in a musical equivalent of slapstick. In the title track, a string sextet, Bermel shows a more serious side, and it is possible to detect a strong blues and gospel influence in the viola’s opening lament, from which everything else in the piece is derived. There is much in the contrast between lyricism and activity here to interest the listener, with the ‘rub’ (as Bermel calls it) of combined European diatonicism and African pentatonicism – of course at the heart of the gospel tradition, with its heightened use of controlled dissonance. A similar culture clash is brought about in Wanderings for woodwind quartet, where Bermel (who studied in Jerusalem) portrays the Old City’s neighbouring Jewish and Muslim quarters in the first movement, Gift of Life. There is certainly some klezmer influence here, but Bermel is notable for integrating this almost seamlessly with the sounds of Arab music so as to sum up the experience as an unified whole. We then move to Nandom in Ghana for the second movement, which treats two gyil songs in a jazzy fashion. Hungary is at the heart of Mulatash Stomp for violin, clarinet and piano, an early work and one of the most attractive on the disc. The mulatas is an all-night Hungarian party, and to bring some American influence to the piece Bermel adds a techno rhythm. Clearly Mozart is also a guest, for a theme from the Jupiter symphony makes much of the running as the piece goes on. There is a great deal to intrigue and stimulate in Bermel’s music, and this disc of fine perform- ances is an excellent way to discover his style. Not only is his music well-crafted, it has a quirky sense of humour and a lightness of touch that should ensure that it finds immediate appeal in the concert hall. John Kersey  73 https://www.cambridge.org/core/terms. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0040298203290173

PARMEGIANI: Capture éphémère; Sons-jeu; La mémoire des sons. INA c 2019. This new Bernard Parmegiani compilation features reissued and original material. Capture éphémère dates from 1967 and previously appeared on one of two Parmegiani releases issued on the legendary Philips series ‘Prospective 21st siècle’, more than four decades ago. A gritty and atmospheric study in textural transformations, it shows Parmegiani steering a middle ground between the opposed aesthetics of Schaeffer and Xenakis, combining sudden cuts and transitions with gradual dispersions of uniformly granular material. During the later sequences of this work the sound masses are laminated to an extraordinary degree of density, creating a glistening, metallic surface which is almost impenetrable. The uncompromising, almost sculptural style and the work’s unprece- dented synthesis of ideas concerning the nature of musique concrète, have served as touchstones of influence for many younger composers. The recent works, Sons-jeu and Mémoires des sons date from 1987 and 2002 respectively. Since both works postdate Parmegiani’s apocalyptic masterpiece La création du monde (1982–4) they are inevitably seen in its monolithic shadow. In no sense, however, are they diminished by compar- ison. At a duration of just over 20 minutes each, both works enact spacious textural transitions which create the sense of a much vaster time scale and evoke richly detailed spatial perspectives. Both works are characteristic of Parmegiani in combining very slow rates of change with sudden, cataclysmic upheavals; and in using disembodied, familiar sounds as raw material for selective transformation and abstraction. Several minutes into Mémoires des sons one hears a loop of distant church bells tolling. The pitches are gradu- ally filtered off, leaving only a disembodied reso- nance which hovers high above a thunderous, wind-like roar. By dissociating resonance from pitch Parmegiani suspends the bell sounds in a timeless void, an empty, transitional space situ- ated between the known and the unknown, between abstraction and representation. At the same time he forms a bridge or continuum between blocks of contrasting mate- rial. During a long transitional sequence the two layers of sound gradually coalesce and then diverge again, splitting into two new layers – one composed of ephemeral, metallic impulses and watery explosions and the other composed of plunging bass tones. Eventually the lower regions assume a quasi-instrumental character, resembling a mass of aboriginal wind instru- ments reverberating inside a cave. The constituent layers then thin away into oblivion and the work ends with characteristic abruptness in a sudden cross-fade in which the wind orchestra is eclipsed by an oceanic surge, like the tide racing over pebbles. The work as a whole seems to emulate the slow, cyclical movements which occur in nature, punctuated by sudden upheavals and disruptions. During the cyclical movements sounds undergo the subtlest of changes, as if occurring by natural metamorphosis rather than as the result of elec- tronic manipulation. Most of these changes are achieved principally by means of cross-fading and superimposition yet the effect is a great deal more complex and subtle than my description indicates. It is Parmegiani’s skill in orchestrating transitions, from the subtlest to the most tempes- tuous, as much as in building lavish sound textures, which makes him the true electroa- coustic heir to the symphonic tradition. Sons-jeu contains much more densely layered changes with various layers endlessly splitting, diverging and re-forming. It is as if one can hear, as through an acoustic microscope, the numerous microscopic changes and divisions occurring within a cellular structure or micro- organism. However, in contradistinction to Mémoire des sons, Sons-jeu features disfigured spoken word material intermodulated with or laminated upon purely electronic sound textures. Both works thereby draw together various thematic strands from Parmegiani’s earlier works. These include the relationship between instrumental and electronic sound, the dichotomy between abstraction and representa- tion, the disfigurement and reconfiguration of spoken language into more abstract forms and the deconstruction and metamorphosis of timbre. It defies comprehension that a composer of such pioneering stature, the author of so many innovative works, remains so under-represented on CD. Many of Parmegiani’s earlier works, which have served as points of reference for more recent developments, were deleted by the end of the 1960s, never to be reissued, while others have never seen the light of day outside of a studio. The deleted works include Bidule en ré (1962), L’oeil écoute (1971) , L’instant mobile (1964), and Ponamotopées II (1964), most of which were released some 40 years ago but are now deserving of the appreciation of a newer, more receptive generation. It is to be hoped that INA will eventually reissue such works and release further material from the earlier stages of a  74 https://www.cambridge.org/core/terms. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0040298203290173

career which stretches back more than half a century. In particular, La table des matières (1979), a panoramic exploration of natural soundscapes and one of Parmegiani’s most compelling and original works, is long overdue for release. Roger Sutherland WYSHNEGRADSKY: Étude on the Rotary Movements, op. 45a;1 24 Preludes in the chromatic scale diatonicised in 13 tones, op. 22. Sylvaine Billier, Martine Joste, 1Gérard Frémy, 1Fuminori Tanada, pianos; 1Fernand Vandenbogaerde, conductor. [All four pianists play in the first work; Billier and Joste play in both.] Col Legno WWE 1CD 20206 In the decades between the world wars, the French-domiciled Russian émigré composer Ivan Wyshnegradsky (1893–1979) was one of several writing ‘microtonal’ music, mostly quarter-tone. But quarter-tone pianos he found inhospitable. Thus the music on this CD requires two pianos each tuned ‘normally’ but a quarter tone from one other. The tuning is not the most interesting aspect of this music. Octaves divided into 24 generally do not produce the most engaging results, even for equal divisions. But Wyshnegradsky explored this tuning with flair. This disc reveals a fine composer, not a dilettante hiding behind an unusual tuning. The short étude (1961), for eight hands, is based on ostinato textures that are elusively tonal. Since quarter-tone melodies may be obtained only by careful alternation of the pianos, they are some- what restricted. The quarter tones in this piece usually come from chords or competing melodic strands. The same problem holds, of course, for the 24 Preludes (1934, revised decades later). But four hands instead of eight mean more interaction is possible between the instruments to create quarter-tone melodies. Longtime Wyshnegradsky exponents Billier and Joste handle the associated performance problems very well. Occasionally, melodies sound slightly uneven in dynamics or rhythm. The preludes reveal the propensity of titles, explanations, translations, and even scores involving Wyshnegradsky to be a challenge. One significant structural unit, for example, is the heptachord, which is translated here as hepta- string. There are two different scores for the preludes. In the performance score, the normal notation for both pianos requires imagining the quarter- tone lowering of the second one. In the study score, the music, accurately notated, goes on one pair of staves only, requiring the reader to untangle which piano plays which notes. The music is in what its composer called ‘the chromatic scale diatonicised in 13 tones’, with the all-time obscurest meaning for diatonic. He does not imply 13 tones to the octave but music based on 13 quarter tones. The octave comple- ment (11 quarter tones) gives a good approxima- tion of the 11th harmonic, which the preludes often emphasize. For a composer not known for dynamic rhythms, Wyshnegradsky’s 4th prelude surprises for its Prokofiev influence. Chopin, Mussorgsky, Debussy, Skryabin, and Schoenberg affect this music too, all positively. The preludes deserve to be heard on one instrument. Except in a few places, they are playable by two hands – if the keyboard is replaced, of course. An ingenious microtonal keyboard configuration, although not for pianos, was invented over a hundred years ago but has not exactly caught on. That’s another story. Paul Rapoport RZEWSKI: Piano Works 1975–1999. Frederic Rzewski (pno). Nonesuch 79623 – 2 (7-CD set). Considering the USA is such a powerful, pros- perous and populous nation, it has produced few outstanding composers in the past 50 years. Elliott Carter and Morton Feldman are obvious exceptions, with their profound understanding of their European heritage. The ideas of John Cage have left a rich legacy for future composers to contemplate. To these may be added Roger Reynolds, with his deep knowledge of Japanese as well as European culture, and Frederic Rzewski, who has pursued much of his career in Europe as pianist, teacher, composer and impro- viser. This seven-disc survey of Rzewski’s piano compositions does not account for every piece – some substantial items are omitted – but they include all the major works written between 1975 and 1999, even if The Road is still incom- plete. The abiding impression is of a composer whose work embodies some intriguing contra- dictions. His piano writing has been influenced by both the ‘classical’ and ‘romantic’ traditions. On the one hand, Rzewski identifies with Bach’s Well-Tempered Klavier, or Mendelssohn’s Songs Without Words; on the other, his immense tech- nique has inevitably drawn him to the virtuoso  75 https://www.cambridge.org/core/terms. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0040298203290173

tradition of Alkan and Liszt. In addition, his tech- nique has been sharpened by collaborations with jazz and improvising musicians, and many of his scores allow for improvised episodes. At the same time, Rzewski has developed a distinctly European sensibility. His profound awareness of postwar ‘modernism’ has encour- aged him to adopt a percussive style, as both composer and interpreter, yet tonality has invari- ably played a major role in his compositions. Hence, his preoccupation with ballads and folk- songs, not least of the United States, even though his political inclinations would find little sympathy in his homeland. Rzewski believes that the best folk and popular melodies are arche- typal, appealing to some innate power of recog- nition within the brain. The five items on the first disc – the Four North American Ballads (1979) and The Housewife’s Lament (1980) – are the most obvious examples. They establish the principle of variation-form, which is fundamental to Rzewski’s composi- tional method, but also illustrate the variety of his approach. Thus, whereas, in Down by the Riverside, the melody is presented at the outset, in Winsboro Cotton Mill Blues, the theme only emerges after the graphic depiction of the mill itself. Disc 2 continues the theme of social protest, expands on the variation principle, and intro- duces some of Rzewski’s stricter compositional procedures. The 24 Variations on the traditional Jewish tune Mayn Yingele (1989) is on a larger scale than anything on the first disc, but is still remarkably compact. The concision of the theme is reflected in the variations, yet the work encompasses a wide range of expression. Further contrast is provided by the inclusion of an extended cadenza, which introduces an impro- visatory element. It can be regarded as ‘a piece within a piece’, as it comprises a freer exploration of much the same ground. A Life (1992) is Rzewski’s memorial to John Cage, conceived in direct response to 4’33”. It is not a silent piece, but its improvisatory character suggests that it could be a possible interpretation of Cage’s instructions. By contrast, Fougues (1994) is one of Rzewski’s most ‘abstract’ compo- sitions. The 25 segments are laid out as varia- tions, and their durations are quite similar; but there is no overriding theme. Likewise, despite the title, there are no fugal episodes. Yet the work is carefully organized. It begins and ends in C major, and Rzewski adopts the same ‘tonal’ system as Chopin in his Preludes. Yet an unequiv- ocal sense of tonality is restricted to the final section. Each section is subdivided into three 15- second phrases, but allowance is made for a degree of spontaneity, and this accounts for an element of flexibility in performance. An analogous outlook can be applied to the recent Fantasia (1999), which opens Disc 3. Improvised and notated passages are in a state of constant interaction, so that echoes of Bach or Chopin are juxtaposed with Rzewski’s individual brand of pianism. His Piano Sonata also explores the borderline between tonality and atonality, improvisation and rigid construction, develop- mental and variation techniques. An introduc- tion and coda ‘frame’ the first movement, but the discourse gives no indication of the underlying scheme, whereby the material in the first 32 of 64 twenty-second units is then telescoped into 16, 8, and 4 sections. Tonal allusions abound, as the movement is based on six popular melodies from different centuries. One of these is L’Homme Armé, whose recurrence in the finale as the basis of a more conventional sequence of variations helps to unify the work. The central movement also has military connotations, based as it is on the bugle call, ‘Taps’. It is also distantly related to the opening movement insofar as it is subdivided into 12 equal periods. There are also thematic links, but the music is not subjected to compression in this instance. The Sonata refers to the development of the genre since Haydn, but as Christian Wolff observes in Nonesuch’s excellent booklet, its source material owes nothing to the Western ‘art music’ tradition. Ultimately, it is an attempt to weld ‘high’ and ‘popular’ culture into a single statement. Rzewski’s Sonata has little to do with tradi- tional musical narrative. The Road (1995–), by contrast, has sufficient narrative elements for the composer to regard it as a ‘novel’. However, it is not indebted to Jack Kerouac’s On the Road. In American lore, the road – and the railroad – have immense symbolic value; and thus The Road can be regarded as Rzewski’s most ‘American’ work. Discs 4 and 5 are devoted to the first four parts of this ongoing ‘work in progess’. The Road is ulti- mately intended to comprise eight parts, each specifically titled; but it is not ‘programme music’. Each individual part is sub-divided into eight movements, yet within this overall scheme, the music is free-wheeling. The work calls for considerable virtuosity, which contradicts Rzewski’s claaim that the music was designed primarily for home consumption. There are improvisatory elements, as well as extra-pianistic activities such as whistling, declaiming, drum- ming on the lid or frame of the instrument, and operating other sonic objects. Popular materials  76 https://www.cambridge.org/core/terms. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0040298203290173

are frequently used in conjunction with standard forms – but in a few, more complex sections, both are avoided. The 36 Variations on The People United will never be Defeated! is the oldest work in this collection (1975), and has already acquired the status of a modern masterpiece. Rzewski’s starting-point was Sergio Ortega’s celebrated song – protesting against Fascism generally, but specifically against the threat posed by the CIA to the democrati- cally-elected Chilean regime of Salvador Allende. The 36 Variations was originally conceived to be performed alongside Beethoven’s Diabelli Variations, and this may partly explain why it remains one of his most carefully organized scores. After a brief introduction, which establishes the main tonal area, the theme is heard twice. The 36 variations are arranged in six cycles of six: the first five cycles emphasize particular musical characteristics – rhythms, melodies, harmonies, etc. The final cycle summarizes the material of the previous five, the first variation summing up the equivalent variations of the preceding cycles; the second alluding to the other second varia- tions, and so on. The work generally follows a trajectory from simplicity to complexity, and includes references to other protest songs, notably Hanns Eisler’s Solidaritätslied. Towards the end, two cadenzas introduce an impro- visatory element, and the coda is a grand recapit- ulation of Ortega’s theme. The People United is an attempt to incorporate the various facets of Rzewski’s creative and inter- pretative activity into a single, unified statement. His political convictions are expressed through the influences of European modernism, jazz, and popular culture; but the basis of his pianistic and compositional virtuosity is a ‘romantic’ sensi- bility. Hence, it is appropriate that the final disc – also the shortest of the set – should be devoted to De Profundis (1992), in which Rzewski declaims, to his own accompaniment, portions of Oscar Wilde’s Letter to Lord Alfred Douglas, written while in Reading Gaol. Rzewski has always shown a keen interest in theatre, notably in a series of scores involving the declamation of texts. Essentially, De Profundis is a melodrama, in which eight sections for voice and piano alternate with eight episodes for piano, frequently accom- panied by a variety of vocal xclamations. Genuine dramatic power is achieved by inte- grating the whole into a single, 30-minute span. Rzewski displays both acting ability and pianistic virtuosity in the way he responds to Wilde’s wide-ranging text, and the result is surprisingly compelling. These seven discs demonstrate that The People United is not the only work by which Frederic Rzewski deserves to be known. The influence of his unique pianism means that there is a remark- able continuity between interpretation and creation, which finds expression in the explo- ration of the borderland between improvisation and composition; and by using popular material, he is constantly traversing the boundary between tonality and atonality. Many pianists have been drawn to Rzewski’s music, and there have been some fine recordings, not least the composer’s own earlier releases. Nevertheless, the virtuosity of his performances on this new set ensure that they are probably as definitive as it is possible to achieve. John Warnaby TALBOT: ‘…similarities between diverse things…’; Blue cell; minus 1500; String Quartets nos. 1 and 2; The Dying Swan; 6/11/98; Falling. The Duke Quartet; Apollo Saxophone Quartet; Joby Talbot (pno/cond.); Rob Farrer (vib/perc); Everton Nelson, Jonathan Carney, Natalia Bonner (vlns); Joel Hunter (vla); Chris Worsey (vlc); Philip Sheppard (vlc/electric vlc); Lucy Shaw (db); Joanna Cackett (bsn); Ivor Talbot (guit. samples). Black Box BBM 1078. Having first come across Joby Talbot as the co- writer, arranger and performer of the music of The Divine Comedy and composer of the devilishly dark scores behind the television series The League of Gentlemen I was intrigued to hear this disc of his chamber music. If the media works of Talbot present an extro- vert face, with influences of Scott Walker, British light music and a cutting sense of humour all on display, then the works on this disc must be regarded as the manifestations of a more interior dialogue, a private music far removed from the more overt if at times breathtakingly subtle world of Talbot’s media and popular music. It is rather as if one had peeled back a layer to expose the naked Talbot within, producing music that exhibits complex passions and that explores a predominantly dark universe. At the same time, I detect a somewhat unformed quality to some of these works, a perhaps deliberate fascination with surfaces that do not allow the listener beyond their mirrored facades, and at times a simplicity of gesture that surely owes something to the popular tradition. Over a long-breathed phrase, Talbot will weave a magically suspended texture (as in part 1 of The Dying Swan) in which it seems for ages as if  77 https://www.cambridge.org/core/terms. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0040298203290173

nothing will actually happen in developmental terms, and then suddenly he will produce a change of chord that takes your breath away. This is music that is unassuming and often undemonstrative, but that turns simple, elemental materials into drama that is absorbing and hard to forget. My favourite of the works on this disc is the suite from The Dying Swan, written as the score to a silent Russian film of 1916, and scored for piano trio. There is a Nymanesque feel to moments of this music, but the overall effect is very much Talbot’s own. The use of space and figuration plays with the listener’s concept of time, so that it feels like a much bigger work than its 35 minute duration. An immediate connexion is apparent with the elegiac mood of 6/11/98 for piano, an effectively poignant short piece written to commemorate Talbot’s wedding. The solo electric cello piece Falling, written for Philip Sheppard, presents an interesting sound- world where the cello is augmented by a recorded guitar sample. Here, Talbot’s use of the medium and its sustaining capabilities produces a texture where polyphonic capabilities are real- ized to the full, creating an intensely atmospheric vision that culminates in the repeated guitar chords, providing a rhythmic and harmonic anchor to the cello’s three-note figure. This is an intense piece that suggests much dramatically; it is not ‘film music’, but rather music about which a film could readily be made. It leads naturally on to the Second String Quartet, which inhabits similar territory, but which ends abruptly after four minutes as if in mid-narrative. Talbot’s music repays repeated listening and a number of the works on this disc certainly stick in the memory. He has a decidedly individual voice, and there are many special moments in his music that touch the listener and cause one to hope for more releases like this one. John Kersey ‘No Title Required’. Perhaps the most important omission from my series of reviews of women composers (cf Tempo 210, 211, 216, 217) was, by virtue of a lack of recent recordings, the South African-born Priaulx Rainier (1903–86). She is best known still for her 1939 String Quartet, available with three other chamber works on Redcliffe (RR007; Redcliffe have also issued her Requiem (1965–6), though I have not encountered this latter disc). 2003 being Rainier’s centenary, it is to be hoped that broadcasts and recordings will be forthcoming. Metier have started early with half- a-disc devoted to three of her works from 1943–1955. The Suite for clarinet and piano (1943) is also available on disc, from Claremont (CDGSE1504, performed by Oliver de Groote and Albie van Schalwyk), but this newcomer is to be preferred, not just for the accompanying set of Five Pieces for Keyboard and the Viola Sonata. This latter work, composed in 1945, is one of Rainier’s most gripping designs, three cogent movements that take up and develop many of the elements apparent in the Suite. The Bartókian mannerisms are the most prevalent, something that can be heard in the music of her younger contemporary, Elizabeth Maconchy. For all the work’s brevity Rainier, a string player herself, fashioned a viola part of considerable virtuosity, which Bridget Carey delivers with finesse. David Carhart accompanies skilfully, and is heard on his own in the Five Pieces written between 1951 (no. 4) and 1955 (no. 2; the others date from 1952). No programme exists for these pithy and highly expressive works, miniature masterpieces everyone. It is a shame that Metier did not feel Rainier merited a disc in her own right, but as accompa- niment (taking up just under half the disc but stealing the title) are three pieces by Sadie Harrison. Her previous disc, Metier’s ‘Taking Flight’, was well received in these pages. Although there are no stylistic links between the two women, both were born in the southern hemisphere (Rainier in South Africa, Harrison in Australia) and made their home in London; I also cannot quite escape the feeling that were Rainier in her mid-30s in 2002, her idiom might not be so far away from Harrison’s. No Title Required is perhaps my personal favourite amongst all the pieces of Harrison’s I have heard. Composed in 1994 for Double Image, it is a diptych for a quintet of flute, clarinet and piano trio. Although the title came from a political poem by Polish Nobel laureate Wisl⁄awa Szymborska, the music is not derived from it at all. The first part is, in the composer’s words, ‘fast and virtuosic, the second, lyrical and colouristic. Both have the same formal pattern – a series of variations where one aspect of each section provides the “theme” for the following variation’. While her separation of each part’s facets is true enough, it must be said that the scoring of the first move- ment is possessed of its own distinctive colouring, while the second is just as virtuosic, in its own way, as the first. The flute solo Three Expositions (1997) is a very different type of piece to No Title Required and not nearly as developed or fully realized. As a test piece or study of flute technique it is of interest, but formally the musical thread seems a little thin in places. Carola Neilinger plays it for all its worth, but the music does not really ignite. After Colonna (2001), by contrast, does just that. The composer’s note tells the inspiration came from ‘the fifteenth century mythological romance, the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili (meaning “the strife of love in a dream”) … presumably authored by the infamous friar, Francesco Colonna’. Here, the structure does derive in part from the literary source, though there are other influences at work (e.g. Skryabin’s Tenth Sonata). After Colonna proves to be somewhere in between its two companion pieces in expressive effect – part- ensemble piece (i.e. duo), part-solo study for the cello, brilliantly thrown off by Miriam Lowbury. Alwynne Pritchard’s musical voice is rather more radical than Harrison’s (or, indeed, Rainier’s). Listening through Metier’s new album of her work, ‘Invisible Cities’, I was struck by its expressive variety, the best of which – at least on this disc – is to be found in her piano pieces, which form the backbone of the programme. The concluding (title) track (from 1999) and the diptych Der Zwerg (‘The Dwarf’, 1996–8) are both fine concert works that deserve wider advo- cacy than may be afforded by a contemporary specialism, however cultish. For all its fluency, Der Zwerg’s compositional history is fairly convo- luted: it started in 1996 with a piece called  79 https://www.cambridge.org/core/terms. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0040298203290173

Mesarch, a ‘musical response to the work of the visual artist James Hugonin’. Two years later this was recast as the second panel of the diptych, Er spricht, and appended to another reworking, from 1997, of a piece originally derived from a Schubert song. Despite their apparently unre- lated inspirations, the two parts sit beautifully together. Invisible Cities itself is a more integrated whole: Pritchard herself describes it as ‘a maze or puzzle, setting the pianist musical problems which he must solve in order to give what he considers to be a “successful” performance of the work’. This, too, has an overt extra-musical source – Italo Calvino’s book of the same title, or rather its final sentence, which is quoted in frag- ments on each page throughout the score. Where words or punctuation marks are common, those pages can be interchanged, providing ‘several possible routes by which the pianist may travel through the piece and possible solutions to the puzzle of the music’s overall form and structure’. There is a danger with such a conceit that the result can end up tritely contrived but – certainly in Ian Pace’s expert hands – Pritchard adroitly avoids this. The result is convincing and compelling. So, too, is the Ivesian Spring (1996), written for Michael Finnissy’s 50th birthday. A one-minute-long trifle, it packs in a good deal. No small part of these works’ effect is due to Pace’s brilliant perform- ances. Not every piece on the disc is as successful as these. Matrix (2001), another maze-like piece, fails to avoid the pitfalls Invisible Cities skirted. Scored for unaccompanied electric violin, it is full of sonorities both intriguing and discomforting; I suspect many will not take to the squeaking and farting noises that interrupt the musical flow. Something similar occurs, though with delib- erate rather than unintentionally humorous effect, in Kit (1999). Written for children, this voice-and-electric-guitar duo is as much a montage as a though-composed work, though the complexities of its flexible approach may prove too awkward for children to perform. Pritchard herself takes on the solo vocal role with aplomb. Guitarist Alan Thomas is heard on the acoustic instrument in Nostos Ou Topos (‘Return to Nowhere’, 2000), another diptych in three overlaid movements: the horizontal (rather than vertical) disposition of the movements requires the piece to be navigated twice (by different courses). Although this work does not convince me in the way Invisible Cities does, it can hardly be grasped on a handful of hearings and it may be that, like the piano quintet Barbara Allen (2000), its subtleties will only be unlocked with time. This last piece is an expansion of a miniature written for the Schubert Ensemble’s Chamber Music 2000 project for children; it draws inspira- tion and material from the folksong and the words set to it, recounting a colliery disaster in the 1830s. The composer describes it as ‘brittle, almost nostalgic’ and in texture it makes a very different impact to its companion pieces. In an informative booklet conversation between Pritchard and Ian Pace, the composer describes how in the clarinet, violin and cello trio Der Glücklose Engel (1999) she ‘was concerned with “expressing the inexpressible”, implying extreme states, rather than actually presenting a listener with the “fulfilment” of an idea’. This quote hits the nail squarely on the head and explains perhaps why this work – a valuable addi- tion to the repertoire as it is scored for E flat clar- inet – is less successful than it might be. Even Pritchard herself confesses that it has a ‘sense of loss that interests me less now than it did then’. The performances and recordings on both Metier discs are uniformly excellent, unlike New World’s new release of music by Gloria Coates. Metier’s discs are all recent studio recordings, albeit that – as with the Pritchard works – they tailored each piece to specific locations; New World’s derive from either a live concert held in 1992 or, in the case of Fragment from Leonardo’s Notebooks, ‘Fonte di Rimini’ a studio account made prior to a 1984 concert performance. Notwithstanding these circumstances, the sound quality is perfectly adequate, though the performances are inevitably a little more rough- and-ready. Coates is something of an outsider: an American unknown in her native country, a foreigner in her adopted one, Germany – though local label CPO have made considerable amends. She is also something of a musical maverick in her structural use of the glissando as a basic building-block. Furthermore her music possesses a single-minded quality that reminded me strongly of Ruggles or Allan Pettersson (it ‘hammers away within well-defined limits’, according to Coates’s apologist Kyle Gann in the booklet). The music sounds nothing like either of those composers, or even Penderecki in his early avant garde phase – rather more perhaps like that of Alois Hába, though without the Czech’s life- affirming exuberance. The unrelieved dissonance of Coates’s glissando-style will put her work beyond the pale for most casual listeners, but there is no denying a curious lyrical beauty to many passages in, for example, the unfortunately titled Cette Blanche Agonie (1988) with its haunting  80 https://www.cambridge.org/core/terms. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0040298203290173

cor anglais solos, or her hypnotic Eighth Symphony Indian Sounds (1991). For this listener at any rate, that beauty is often undermined by a deliberate avoidance of contrast and a single-minded intensity that borders on the stubborn. (Even the symphony’s three movement titles emphasize this: Indian Grounds, Indian Mounds and Indian Rounds.) The use of pentatonic melodies and chanted texts from three North American tribes does give the work a distinctive atmosphere, quite different to those of the other symphonies I have heard by this composer. The vocal parts, however, are not the centre of focus, but rather a quasi-instru- mental line that contributes to the whole. In many of Coates’s vocal works, it is the music the texts generate that is important, attaining a status greater than that of mere accompaniment – indeed, she is often uninterested in the audibility of the words set. This attitude could seem self- defeating, were it not for the undoubted sincerity of her approach. Cette Blanche Agonie is a case in point: more a fantasia or tone poem for two soloists, one of whom happens to be a singer of verses by Mallarmé. Likewise for Wir Tönen Allein (1988), a small cantata for soprano and chamber orchestra setting one of Paul Celan’s last poems. By contrast, the impressionistic concluding Fragment from Leonardo’s Notebooks, ‘Fonte di Rimini’ (1976, rev. 1984: recorded here in presum- ably the first performance of that revision) uses the four voices in a consciously colouristic manner in a setting of an epigrammatic note of Leonardo da Vinci: Create a harmony with the different falls of water, as you have seen them at the fountain of Rimini (on the 8th day of August, 1502). In the cantata for soprano and chamber orchestra, The Force for Peace in War (1973), Coates deliberately toned down her style, broad- ening the music’s appeal and accessibility and ending in a broadly tonal plea for peace. The work was partially a reaction to her duties as a US Forces tour guide based in Munich, where her itinerary regularly took her to Dachau; and partially a protest against US involvement in the Vietnam War. The references to the Holocaust drew strong protests early on, though she was attacked more as an American, a woman and a setter of texts by women! This sequence of three recitatives, four arias and orchestral interlude (‘Hiroshima is Bombed’) is very much of its time, but still makes a vivid impact. As mentioned above, the performances and sound quality are variable, but the disposition of the works on the disc is more worthy of comment. The Force for Peace in War and the Leonardo Fragment are the pieces most likely to appeal to a general listener, so I think it an error to begin with one of her most idiosyncratic creations, Cette Blanche Agonie: many may be put off from a casual hearing of track 1. Rather, I would have opened with the orchestral tone painting of the Leonardo Fragment, and followed this with The Force for Peace in War. Cette Blanche Agonie and Wir Tönen Allein, both written in the same year, could then form an effectively contrasting pair preparing for the disc’s longest – and genuinely major – item, the Eighth Symphony. As it is, I think the present sequence does Coates no favours and strips the symphony of some of its stature. This is a shame, for other- wise the works here would make a reasonable introduction to the sound-world and work of this very individual creative voice.
